blocks.md: An average can change even when nobody's pay changes, simply because the mix of people in the group shifts. If more college graduates go on to earn master's degrees, the average college wage rises even though every individual wage stays the same. Composition adjustment removes that effect by averaging with a fixed mix of people over time, so a change in the average reflects a real change in pay rates rather than a change in who is in the group.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: Without it, a rising wage gap might just reflect a changing workforce rather than a changing price of skill.
Holding the mix of sub-groups fixed when averaging, so that a measured change reflects **prices**, not **shifts in who is in the group**.

A group average is a weighted average of sub-group averages ([Law of Iterated Expectations](note:law-of-iterated-expectations)). If the weights change, the average moves even when no sub-group's wage moves.
Take data at the year × detailed-education level, with $e \in \mathcal{E}_H$ (college) or $e \in \mathcal{E}_L$ (non-college), sample weights $s_{ey}$ and average wages $w_{ey}$.
Both are ratios of average wages; only the weights differ.
No wage changes. College workers shift from $e_2$ toward the higher-paid $e_3$ (think: more postgraduate degrees).

| | 1990 | 2000 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Not adjusted | 1.75 | **2.00** |
| Adjusted (base-year weights 0.25, 0.25) | 1.75 | 1.75 |
| Adjusted (period-average weights 0.125, 0.375) | 1.875 | 1.875 |
The unadjusted premium "rises" purely from composition. The adjusted one correctly shows no change in prices. The *level* depends on which fixed weights you pick; the *change* does not.

When you want the **price** of skill — what the same worker would earn — rather than the average earnings of whoever happens to be in the group. That is what the [Skill Premium](note:skill-premium) in the [Canonical Model of the Skill Premium](note:canonical-model-of-the-skill-premium) needs. In practice, cells are defined by education × experience × gender etc.
The composition change does not vanish — it shows up as more college labour **supply** in efficiency units. See [Efficiency Units of Labor](note:efficiency-units-of-labor).

The same idea applies to inequality. Total variance of log wages is a share-weighted sum of within-cell variances and squared gaps between cell means ([Within- and Between-Group Inequality](note:within-and-between-group-inequality)). If the workforce shifts toward cells with higher variance or more extreme means, total variance rises even when no cell's wages change. Fixing the shares removes that:
**Worked example** — two cells, no change in any cell's wages: non-college (mean log wage 2.5, variance 0.15) and college (mean 3.0, variance 0.25). The college share rises from 0.2 to 0.4.

| | Year 1 | Year 2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Within part | 0.170 | 0.190 |
| Between part | 0.040 | 0.060 |
| Total variance | 0.210 | **0.250** |
| Composition-adjusted (year-1 shares) | 0.210 | 0.210 |
The whole rise of 0.04 is composition: more workers in the group with more dispersed wages, and a more even split between groups with different means.
